## Why I built this

I worked in environmental consulting for six years, where a lot of trend analysis still defaults to a straight line through the data because that's what's fast and familiar. Partway through a Master of Data Science, I started running into methods — piecewise regression, changepoint detection, GAMs — that would have changed how I read several records I'd already reported on, if I'd known them going in. This site is my attempt to connect those two sides: write up the methods the way I wish someone had explained them to me before I needed them, grounded in the kind of water-quality data an environmental consultant actually works with day to day.

As recommended by USEPA ProUCL for temporal trends, common practice is to use log-transformed ordinary least squares (OLS) to assess linearity, which I've worked through in a synthetic exercise in a separate repository here: [github.com/iangault/vignette-temporal-trends](https://github.com/iangault/vignette-temporal-trends).

The case studies use simulated data. I used Claude Code to help with drafting and code review, and reviewed and edited everything it produced.

Much of the statistical framing here draws on UBC Master of Data Science coursework, particularly DSCI 561: Regression I, DSCI 562: Regression II, and DSCI 571: Supervised Learning I (see [References](#references)). The application to environmental monitoring is my own.

## Why nonlinear methods matter here

Environmental data rarely behaves as neatly as the models used to describe it. A straight-line trend is a fine description when a concentration is genuinely rising or falling at a constant rate — but many real records don't look like that: a flat baseline that suddenly starts climbing, a level that jumps once and holds, a rise that levels off into a plateau, a seasonal cycle riding on top of a slower trend. Forcing a straight line onto any of these shapes produces a technically-fitted but practically misleading answer: it can make a plateaued analyte look like it's still climbing, or smear a one-time step change into what reads as a gradual trend.

This site opens with two foundational chapters: a general regression framework for abstracting from raw data to a model - choosing a structure that actually matches the shape in front of you — ([The Regression Framework](chapters/regression-framework.qmd)), and a toolkit for diagnosing whether an apparent nonlinearity comes from the regressor or from the distribution of the response, and which transformation fixes it ([Transformations](chapters/transformations.qmd)).

The chapters that follow are organized by who decides the curve's shape, rather than by how flexible each method is. [Piecewise regression](chapters/piecewise-regression.qmd) and [changepoint detection](chapters/changepoint-detection.qmd) still let the analyst pick where a break is and what kind it is, fitting coefficients around that choice.

[k-Nearest neighbors](chapters/knn-regression.qmd) and [LOESS](chapters/loess-smoothing.qmd) hand that decision to the data instead — they diagnose the record's shape with no assumed form, but neither one produces a significance test for the shape it finds.

[GAM](chapters/gam.qmd) keeps the data-driven shape and adds that test, with the flexibility controlled by a fitted penalty rather than an assumed form. [GAMM](chapters/gamm.qmd) then checks whether that test can be trusted once residuals are correlated.

Two closing chapters turn from fitting to choosing. [Linear vs. Nonlinear Comparison](chapters/linear-vs-nonlinear-comparison.qmd) checks whether added flexibility was worth it against a plain linear fit, and goes through a case study of when it's not. [Mechanism vs. Shape](chapters/mechanism-vs-shape.qmd) asks what a fitted curve entitles an analyst to say, fitting Total Phosphorus three ways (logistic, piecewise, GAM) and contrasting it with a simulated plume whose first-order decay justifies a parametric model.

## What ordinary least squares is actually doing

Ordinary least squares models the conditional mean of the response given the regressors, not the response itself (DSCI 562). For a single predictor:

$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \text{ i.i.d.} \qquad (1)$$

Equivalently, $E[Y \mid X = x] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ means that on average, at a given value of $x$, expect this response value of $y$ — a claim about the average trajectory, not any individual point.

The core assumptions, roughly in order of how much trouble breaking them causes:

- **Linearity** — the true conditional mean really is a straight line in the predictors. This is the assumption every method on this site is about testing or relaxing.
- **Independence** — residuals aren't correlated with each other. Time-ordered data like these water-quality records are especially prone to violating this: a value close to the last one tends to stay close, producing autocorrelated residuals that standard OLS doesn't account for ([GAMM](chapters/gamm.qmd) addresses this later).
- **Homoscedasticity** — how far the observed response scatters around its fitted conditional mean is assumed to stay constant across the range of $x$, not narrower at low values and wider at high ones (or vice versa).
- **Normality of errors** — this assumption applies to the error term $\varepsilon_i$ in equation (1). Since equation (1) defines $y_i$ as $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$ plus $\varepsilon_i$, a normal $\varepsilon_i$ forces $y_i$ to be normal too, centered on $\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$ instead of 0. What this assumption buys is valid $t$- and $F$-tests even at small sample sizes. Those tests work by comparing an estimate like $\hat\beta_1$ against its sampling distribution — the distribution of values $\hat\beta_1$ would take if the same study were repeated over and over on new samples — and that sampling distribution is only exactly normal when the underlying errors are exactly normal. At large sample sizes the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) — the result that a sum or average of many independent random quantities tends toward a normal distribution regardless of the shape of each one individually — makes the sampling distribution of $\hat\beta_1$ approximately normal anyway, so the assumption matters most when the sample is small.

## A model is an abstraction, not a recovery

Every method here — linear, piecewise, LOESS, GAM — is a different simplification of an unknown true process. Environmental modelling has largely given up the assumption that a single correct representation of a system can be identified from the data normally available (Beven, 2006). The relevant question is which simplification is adequate for the decision at hand and cheap enough to explain and defend. A straight line is a fine abstraction when the data really is monotonic; it becomes actively misleading once the shape genuinely bends.

## Inference vs. prediction

Two different jobs a model can do, and every case study on this site is doing the first one:

- **Inference** — the coefficients themselves are the answer: is there a real trend, how big is it, is it statistically distinguishable from noise. This requires the model form to be roughly right, since a misspecified model gives confident-looking, wrong numbers.
- **Prediction** — only $\hat y$ for new inputs matters; the model can be an uninterpretable black box as long as it's accurate out-of-sample.

Not every method here can do inference, and that's a structural property of the fitting procedure. For this site:

- **Inference-capable, and therefore prediction-capable too:** linear regression, piecewise/segmented regression, changepoint detection, GAM, GAMM. Each produces an interpretable, testable parameter — a slope, a breakpoint location, a shift, a significance test on a smooth term — and the same fit gives a $\hat y$ for free.
- **Prediction-only, structurally:** k-nearest-neighbors and LOESS. Neither ever produces a coefficient or a p-value — there is no mechanism for one to come out of. What they supply is $\hat y$ within the observed range of $x$.

## Types of models

Model choice is a tradeoff along three axes:

- **Interpretability** — can the fitted model be explained to a non-statistician
- **Fit quality** — does it capture the actual shape
- **Data efficiency** — how much data it needs to estimate reliably

The methods on this site sit on a spectrum from parametric to nonparametric, and the spectrum tracks who is deciding the functional form:

- **Parametric** (linear, piecewise) — the analyst picks a small, fixed number of parameters and a specific form (a slope, a hinge). Highly interpretable and cheap to estimate, but correct only if the true shape matches the assumed form.
- **Nonparametric, used diagnostically** (k-nearest-neighbors, LOESS) — no fixed functional form; the fit adapts to local structure so the analyst can see the shape before committing to one. Needs more data to estimate as reliably as a correctly-specified parametric model, and doesn't by itself reduce to a handful of reportable numbers or a significance test. Reviews of water-quality trend methods describe smoothing in the same terms: flexible, but still largely descriptive (Esterby, 1996).
- **Semi-parametric** (GAM) — smooth basis functions like LOESS, but with a fitted penalty controlling how much wiggle is allowed, plus proper inferential machinery LOESS doesn't provide. This is the route for shapes like Total Copper's step-and-spike pattern, where nothing about the system fixes the curve's form in advance. When something does, such as first-order decay after a source is removed, a parametric model built on that mechanism is the stronger choice ([Mechanism vs. Shape](chapters/mechanism-vs-shape.qmd)).

### Nonparametric definitions

"Nonparametric" has two distinct meanings in trend analysis, and this site only uses one of them.

In **hypothesis testing**, a nonparametric test is one that makes no assumption about the **distribution of the errors**. **Mann-Kendall** is the standard example: it works on ranks rather than raw values, so it doesn't require normally-distributed residuals the way a t-test does. But it still makes a claim about the **functional form**: it assumes the relationship being tested is **monotonic**: a change with no reversals of direction, which may happen steadily, in steps, or in any other pattern that does not change sign (Hirsch et al., 1991). It has no way to describe what shape that change took, because "monotonic" is the only shape built into the test. It can flag Total Chloride's straight-line trend, and Total Phosphorus's rise-then-plateau is monotonic too, so it would likely flag that increase as well, without showing that the record levelled off. A record that reverses direction, like Total Copper's, is where it can fail outright: a non-monotonic change can go undetected by methods sensitive only to monotonic change (Esterby, 1996).

In **curve-fitting**, which is how "nonparametric" is used everywhere else on this site, it means there's no single equation tying the fitted value at one $x$ to the fitted value at another — a nonparametric fit like k-NN or LOESS **estimates the curve's height locally** from nearby data points instead, with no commitment to any fixed shape, monotonic or not. That's what lets it represent a plateau or a bend as easily as a straight line. It's the **functional form** that's left unassumed here, not the error distribution — the opposite of what "nonparametric" leaves unassumed in the hypothesis-testing sense above.

## Why this matters for a client or regulator

Model choice changes what gets reported and what action follows. A plateau misread as ongoing growth can trigger a treatment upgrade or permit renegotiation nobody actually needed. A step change misread as a gradual trend sends the investigation toward the wrong cause — a slow watershed process instead of the operational event or permit change that actually happened — and delays the fix. And a flexible model fit to pure noise manufactures a trend that isn't there, triggering escalation over nothing. The reverse failure carries its own cost: real change dismissed as noise because the model wasn't flexible enough to see it. Guarding against both means using the model whose complexity is actually supported by the data — no more, no less — and being able to explain that choice in plain terms to someone who isn't a statistician, since a result nobody can sanity-check doesn't get trusted enough to act on.

## Start from the goal, not the method

The default reflex, faced with any time series, is to fit a straight line through it. That reflex is itself a form of model misspecification whenever the record isn't actually a straight line. The water-quality trend literature puts the objective first: the suitable method depends on how trend is defined, how the other sources of variability are modelled, the characteristics of the data, and the objectives of the monitoring program (Esterby, 1996). Environmental modelling more broadly starts the same way, with the purpose of the model (Kelly et al., 2013). This site offers a set of starting points, one per goal, each demonstrated on a case study built to need it, rather than one recommended method. The table below maps the goal to the chapter.

[The Regression Framework](chapters/regression-framework.qmd) and [Transformations](chapters/transformations.qmd) aren't tied to any one row above — they're the shared vocabulary and diagnostic checks every method in the table depends on.

| What you're trying to find out | Purpose | Definition | Start here | What you get |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I just want to see the shape of the record before committing to any model form | Exploratory | Visualizing local structure with no fitted coefficients | [k-Nearest Neighbors](chapters/knn-regression.qmd) / [LOESS](chapters/loess-smoothing.qmd) | Prediction only, structurally: no coefficient or p-value comes out of either one. [GAM](chapters/gam.qmd) adds a significance test without fixing the shape in advance |
| Is there a real trend at all, or would a flexible model just be fitting noise? | Diagnostic / triage | A general first check, not tied to one shape | [Linear vs. Nonlinear Comparison](chapters/linear-vs-nonlinear-comparison.qmd) | An inference answer: tested against "no added complexity is justified" |
| A permit change or effluent release on a known date may have shifted the slope. Did it, and by how much? | Confirmatory | Quantifying a slope change around a documented event | [Piecewise / Segmented Regression](chapters/piecewise-regression.qmd) | Two slopes and a breakpoint location, each with a confidence interval, and Davies' test for whether the slope changes at all. A break picked out by eye with no event behind it needs that test, since choosing the break from the data biases an ordinary before/after test (Hirsch et al., 1991) |
| There may have been a spill that jumped the level to something new, and I don't know when | Forensic | Locating an unknown event from the data alone | [Changepoint Detection](chapters/changepoint-detection.qmd) | A break location found by search, with a confidence interval and a significance test for whether a break exists at all |
| I have a large dataset with no single knot or known curve to fit, and I need a defensible significance test | General-purpose / flexible-but-inferential | Fitting a smooth curve without assuming its shape in advance | [Generalized Additive Models](chapters/gam.qmd) | A smooth curve with an effective-degrees-of-freedom count and a significance test on the smooth term |
| The record is seasonal or regularly sampled, and residuals might not be independent (e.g. monthly monitoring) | Assumption check | Corrects a GAM's result rather than posing a new goal | [Generalized Additive Mixed Models](chapters/gamm.qmd) | The same smooth-term test as a GAM, with standard errors that account for correlated residuals |
| A curve looks like a known family (decay, saturation, growth). Can I fit that family and report its parameters? | Model choice | Checking whether a known process justifies a parametric form | [Mechanism vs. Shape](chapters/mechanism-vs-shape.qmd) | A rate constant with a CI when a known process holds and its predictions check out; otherwise a GAM description of when the record changed, how fast, and whether it is still changing |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,12,17,17,32]"}


A fitted model from any row above is typically a starting point of its own, not an endpoint — most chapters close with a short note on what a deeper analysis, built on top of what's fitted there, would look like.

## The case studies

Seven analytes, each chosen to demonstrate a specific shape or to act as a control — monthly sampling, single composite site, 2013–2024.

```{r}
#| label: raw-overview
#| fig-height: 8
#| echo: false
ggplot(non_linear_wq |> order_analytes(), aes(date, result)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~analyte, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Result") +
  nlt_theme
```

- **Total Nitrogen** — flat, then a genuine slope break. Piecewise/segmented regression: two slopes, one knot, no discontinuity.
- **Specific Conductance** — a level jump at an unknown location. Changepoint detection: the same "something shifted" question as Total Nitrogen, but without being told where.
- **Total Phosphorus** — a rise that levels into a plateau. Used twice, for k-nearest-neighbors and LOESS on the same data, as a direct side-by-side of two local methods, then revisited in [Mechanism vs. Shape](chapters/mechanism-vs-shape.qmd), where it is fit as a logistic curve, a piecewise model and a GAM, and the GAM reports when the rise happened, how fast it was, and what the record can say about whether it is still rising.
- **Dissolved Oxygen** — a seasonal cycle riding on a longer-term trend, with residuals correlated month to month. GAMM: whether the trend's significance survives once that correlation is modeled explicitly.
- **Total Chloride** — a genuine, unremarkable straight-line trend. A control: the case where the simple linear model is already the right answer.
- **Total Zinc** — pure noise, no real trend. The other control: the guard against a flexible model manufacturing a trend that isn't there.
- **Total Copper** — step-like and non-monotonic: up, up again into a brief spike, back down, further down, then a partial recovery. GAM: a shape with no periodic or polynomial pattern for a hand-built OLS feature to fall back on.
